ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 3: The Seven Churches (continued)
title: The Seven Churches (continued)
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain how Smith reads the last three churches — Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea — as successive historical periods that bring the church ever nearer the second advent, and unpack what Christ's counsel to lukewarm Laodicea (buy gold, white raiment, and eye-salve) actually means.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, what historical bodies and time period does the church of Sardis represent?
options: The apostolic church of the first century
The reformed churches, from about 1798 to the great advent movement
The persecuted believers of the Dark Ages
The final church of the very last generation before Christ's return
questions.explanation: The chapter dates Sardis from about 1798 and says it constitutes "the reformed churches, from the date above named to the great movement which marked another era in the history of the people of God," whose chief fault is having a name to live while being dead.

questions.stem: Regarding the warning to Sardis, "If thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief," how does the chapter say the coming and the manner of the coming relate to watching?
options: Both the coming and its manner are conditional on whether the church watches
The coming is conditional, but its manner is unconditional
The coming is unconditional; only the manner of it (being overtaken as by a thief) is conditional on watching
Neither the coming nor its manner has anything to do with watching
questions.explanation: The text states: "The coming spoken of is unconditional; the manner only in which it would come upon them is conditional. Their not watching would not prevent the coming of the Lord; but by watching they could avoid being overtaken as by a thief."

questions.stem: What does the chapter say the Philadelphian church represents?
options: The medieval church before the Reformation
The position and spirit of those who received the Advent message up to the autumn of 1844
The worldly, self-satisfied churches after 1844
The Gentile believers of the early apostolic era
questions.explanation: The chapter says Philadelphia, meaning "brotherly love," "expresses the position and spirit of those who received the Advent message up to the autumn of 1844," who left party names behind and pointed to the coming of the Son of man.

questions.stem: How does the chapter interpret Christ as the one who "openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth"?
options: As a reference to opening and closing the door of individual hearts in conversion
As Christ's change of ministration in the heavenly sanctuary — opening His work in the most holy place and ceasing it in the holy place — at the close of the 2300 days in 1844
As the opening of the Christian church to the Gentiles
As the opening of the seven seals described later in Revelation
questions.explanation: The chapter ties this language to Christ's sanctuary ministry, explaining that at the close of the 2300 days in 1844 the time came for the cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary: "the opening being the opening of his ministration in the most holy place, and the shutting, its cessation in the first apartment, or holy place."

questions.stem: The chapter argues that the references to Christ's coming grow progressively stronger across the later churches. How does it describe this pattern?
options: All seven churches contain identical warnings about the second coming
Only Laodicea mentions Christ's coming at all

The first three churches have no allusion to the second coming, then Thyatira ("Hold fast till I come"), Sardis (come as a thief), and Philadelphia ("Behold, I come quickly") successively bring it nearer
The earliest churches emphasize the coming most, and the later ones drop the theme
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the first three churches "contain no allusion to the second coming," then traces an increasing emphasis: Thyatira's "Hold fast till I come," Sardis's coming as a thief, and Philadelphia's "Behold, I come quickly," showing the churches "occupy positions successively nearer the great day of the Lord."

questions.stem: What does the chapter identify as the chief fault of the Laodicean church, and why is it so dangerous?
options: Open idolatry and persecution of the faithful, which provokes God's immediate judgment
Holding false doctrines such as those of Balaam or the Nicolaitanes
Lukewarmness combined with self-satisfaction — they think they are rich and need nothing, so they feel no lack to drive them to seek better things
Excessive zeal and fanaticism that misleads the world
questions.explanation: The charge is lukewarmness: "the most discouraging feature of the lukewarm is that they are conscious of no lack, and feel that they have need of nothing." The chapter notes no fault is found with their doctrine; they are content with a correct theory without its power.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter argue that Christ saying "I would thou wert cold or hot" does NOT mean He wishes the church were openly wicked like the world?
options: Because the word "cold" in the original Greek means "hot"

Because Christ would not wish anyone in open rebellion, no state offends Him more than the sinner in rebellion, and the threat of rejection is precisely because they are neither cold nor hot — implying cold would not be rejected
Because the cold are simply unbelievers outside the church who are irrelevant to the message
Because the chapter says Christ never expressed any preference between the states
questions.explanation: The chapter gives three reasons: it would be harsh to have Christ wish anyone in open rebellion; no state offends Christ more than the sinner in open rebellion; and the threat of rejection is because they are neither cold nor hot, which implies the cold would not be rejected. So "cold" denotes a feeling of lack and longing within the church, not worldly wickedness.

questions.stem: How does the chapter interpret the three things Laodicea is counseled to buy — gold tried in the fire, white raiment, and eye-salve?
options: Literal wealth, literal clothing, and literal medicine for the eyes
Faith/hope/love (the gold), the righteousness of saints (white raiment), and the Holy Spirit that quickens spiritual discernment (eye-salve)
Church membership, baptism, and ordination
Prophecy, tongues, and healing as the three spiritual gifts
questions.explanation: The chapter explains the gold as the graces of faith, hope, and charity (1 Corinthians 13); the white raiment as "the righteousness of saints" (Revelation 19:8); and the eye-salve as the Holy Spirit, the one agent that quickens spiritual discernment (the "unction from the Holy One").
